# Day 2: Understanding & Cleaning Clinical Data

## Plan

- Why cleaning matters: garbage in, garbage out
- Variable types and clinical coding
- Missing data, duplicates, inconsistent categories
- Validation, recoding, dates and factors
- Save the clean dataset: the contract for Days 3-5

::: {.notes}
Key point: today we turn a messy raw file into a tidy, analysis-ready dataset and save it once for the whole week.

Misconception: cleaning is not a quick step before the 'real' work; it IS most of the work.

Clinical interpretation: every later result depends on decisions made today.

Ask: who has ever found an error in their data after running the analysis? Expected: most hands go up, often after submission.

Demo tip: keep the raw file open beside the script so people see the mess we are taming.
:::

## Why Data Cleaning Matters

### Garbage in, garbage out

| A p-value cannot rescue a mistyped blood pressure.
| Errors do not announce themselves; they hide in plausible numbers.
| Clean data is the foundation of a credible result.

### How much of a project is cleaning?

| Typically 60-80% of total analysis time.
| Skipping it does not save time; it moves the cost to peer review.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why clinicians should care
A wrong cut-off or unit can flip a clinical conclusion.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: cleaning is the majority of real-world analysis time and the part reviewers scrutinise most.

Misconception: 'the data manager already cleaned it' - someone must still check it against clinical sense.

Clinical interpretation: an SBP of 7 or an age of 200 will quietly distort means and models.

Ask: what is a realistic resting SBP range for an adult? Expected: roughly 90-180; this intuition is exactly what we encode as validation rules.

Demo tip: show one impossible value and ask what it would do to a mean.
:::

## Variable Types in Clinical Data

| Type | What it is | Example in our data |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Continuous | Numbers on a scale | age, sbp\_mmhg, weight\_kg |
| Binary | Two categories | diabetes (Yes/No) |
| Categorical | Unordered groups | facility, occupation |
| Ordinal | Ordered groups | education (None to Tertiary) |
| Date | Calendar time | enroll\_date |

: The type decides how R stores, summarises and models a variable.

::: {.notes}
Key point: choosing the right type up front controls every later summary, plot and model.

Misconception: 'a number is always continuous' - coded categories (1=Yes) are numbers but are categorical.

Clinical interpretation: ordinal education should keep its order; facility should not be treated as a ranked scale.

Ask: is a Likert pain score 0-10 continuous or ordinal? Expected: defensible either way; the point is to decide deliberately.

Demo tip: map each row to a column in the open raw file.
:::

## Clinical Coding: Consistent Codes {.smaller}

### What coding means

| Agreeing one written value per real-world category.
| Sex stored as Female / Male, not F / f / female.
| Binaries stored as Yes / No, not a mix of Y, 1, true.

### Why it matters

| R treats 'Yes' and 'yes' as two different groups.
| Inconsistent codes split one category into several.
| Consistent codes make tables and models trustworthy.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common trap
Eight spellings of sex become eight phantom categories.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: a category exists only if its label is written identically every time.

Misconception: R is smart enough to know 'Y' means 'Yes' - it is not.

Clinical interpretation: a split sex variable would bias any sex-adjusted estimate.

Ask: how many distinct values of sex might a free-text field produce? Expected: surprisingly many; we will see eight.

Demo tip: run table() before cleaning to reveal the chaos.
:::

## Missing Data: How It Hides

### It rarely looks like one thing

| Blank cells, the word NA, and sentinel codes 999 or -99.
| If R does not recognise them, 999 is treated as a real value.
| A single 999 can wreck a mean or a regression.

### Read it correctly at import

| Tell read\_csv which strings mean missing.
| na = c("", "NA", "999", "-99")

::: {.callout-note}
## Types of missingness (brief)
MCAR, MAR, MNAR - the pattern affects how we handle it later.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: define missingness at import so sentinels never enter the analysis as numbers.

Misconception: blanks are the only kind of missing - numeric sentinels are the dangerous ones.

Clinical interpretation: 999 systolic would inflate the mean and falsely raise hypertension prevalence.

Ask: what happens to mean(sbp) if one 999 is read as a real value? Expected: it jumps; the example sells the na= argument.

Demo tip: import once without na= and once with it; compare summary().
:::

## Duplicates: 1503 vs 1500 {.smaller}

### The story

| The raw file has 1503 rows but only 1500 patients.
| Three records were entered twice - exact duplicates.
| Duplicates inflate the sample and distort estimates.

### Detect and remove

| sum(duplicated(raw)) shows how many full duplicates.
| distinct(raw) keeps one copy of each unique row.
| n\_distinct(raw\$patient\_id) should then equal nrow(raw).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Always re-check
Confirm row count is 1500 after distinct().
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: duplicates are a false sample-size increase and must go before any counting.

Misconception: distinct() drops rows you wanted - it only removes exact full-row copies here.

Clinical interpretation: a duplicated patient double-counts their outcome, biasing prevalence.

Ask: why check n\_distinct(patient\_id) as well as nrow? Expected: to catch same-ID-different-row data-entry errors distinct() would keep.

Demo tip: print nrow before and after so the 1503 to 1500 drop is visible.
:::

## Inconsistent Categories: the 8 Spellings of Sex {.smaller}

### The mess

| Female, F, female, f and Male, M, male, m.
| Stray spaces make even more variants.
| Eight labels for two real groups.

### The fix

| str\_trim() removes leading and trailing spaces.
| str\_to\_lower() makes case irrelevant.
| case\_when() maps every variant to Female or Male.

::: {.callout-note}
## Clinical sense
Anything unexpected becomes NA, not a guess.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: normalise case and spacing first, then map a small set of known values.

Misconception: you must list every variant by hand - lowercasing collapses half of them instantly.

Clinical interpretation: never invent a sex for an unreadable entry; NA is honest.

Ask: why send unknowns to NA rather than to the larger group? Expected: guessing introduces bias; NA is transparent.

Demo tip: show table(sex) before and after the case\_when.
:::

## Standardising Binaries with a Helper

[One reusable function fixes every Yes/No variable.]{.slide-intro}

```r
to_yesno <- function(x) {
  x <- str_to_lower(str_trim(as.character(x)))
  case_when(
    x %in% c("yes","y","1","true") ~ "Yes",
    x %in% c("no","n","0","false") ~ "No",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_)
}
raw <- raw |> mutate(across(
  c(diabetes, family_history_htn, health_insurance,
    htn_diagnosed, treatment_uptake), to_yesno))
```

::: {.code-note}
Write the rule once, apply it to many columns with across().
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: a helper function makes the same cleaning rule consistent and auditable across columns.

Misconception: you should repeat case\_when for each variable - across() avoids copy-paste errors.

Clinical interpretation: treatment\_uptake must be a clean Yes/No before it can be an outcome.

Ask: why coerce as.character first? Expected: a column read as numeric 0/1 would not match the text patterns otherwise.

Demo tip: call to\_yesno(c("Y"," no ",1)) on its own to show it working.
:::

## Validation: Impossible Physiological Values

### Spot the impossible

| age 200 and age 0; sbp 0 and sbp 700.
| weight 7 kg; height 17 cm.
| These are data-entry errors, not real patients.

### Fix with plausible ranges

| if\_else(age \>= 18 & age \<= 110, age, NA\_real\_)
| Outside the range becomes NA, not a deletion of the row.

::: {.callout-note}
## Choosing ranges
Set limits from clinical knowledge and your study's population, not from the data alone.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: encode clinical plausibility as explicit ranges and convert violations to NA.

Misconception: outliers and impossible values are the same - a true SBP of 185 is plausible and must stay.

Clinical interpretation: ranges should reflect the population; an adult study justifies age \>= 18.

Ask: should we delete the whole row for one bad height? Expected: no - blank only that cell so the other valid fields survive.

Demo tip: show summary() before and after; the min and max snap into a sensible range.
:::

## Recoding and Deriving Variables

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Recompute BMI from source

- bmi = weight\_kg / (height\_cm/100)\^2
- Derive after cleaning height and weight.
- Never trust a pre-computed BMI blindly.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Create clinical categories

- bmi\_cat with cut(): Underweight to Obese.
- bp\_category with case\_when().
- Normal, Elevated, Hypertension.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Key point: derive variables from cleaned inputs so the derived value inherits the cleaning.

Misconception: recomputing BMI is redundant - the supplied column may be stale or wrong.

Clinical interpretation: bp\_category uses guideline cut-offs (\>=140/90 hypertension, \>=130/80 elevated).

Ask: why recompute BMI instead of keeping the file's column? Expected: it guarantees consistency with the validated height and weight.

Demo tip: show one row where the supplied BMI disagrees with the recomputed value.
:::

## Demo: Recompute BMI and Categorise

```r
raw <- raw |> mutate(
  bmi = round(weight_kg / (height_cm/100)^2, 1),
  bmi_cat = cut(bmi,
    breaks = c(-Inf, 18.5, 25, 30, Inf),
    labels = c("Underweight","Normal",
               "Overweight","Obese")),
  bp_category = case_when(
    is.na(sbp_mmhg) | is.na(dbp_mmhg) ~ NA_character_,
    sbp_mmhg >= 140 | dbp_mmhg >= 90 ~ "Hypertension",
    sbp_mmhg >= 130 | dbp_mmhg >= 80 ~ "Elevated",
    TRUE ~ "Normal"))
```

::: {.code-note}
Handle NA explicitly first so missing BP never reads as Normal.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: order case\_when from most specific to most general, and trap NA before the TRUE branch.

Misconception: NA falls through to the last TRUE branch - so a missing BP would be wrongly labelled Normal.

Clinical interpretation: misclassifying missing BP as Normal would understate hypertension burden.

Ask: what would happen if the is.na line were removed? Expected: patients with missing BP get labelled Normal - a silent error.

Demo tip: deliberately drop the is.na line, run table(bp\_category), then restore it.
:::

## Demo: Parsing Mixed Date Formats

[enroll\_date arrives in several different formats.]{.slide-intro}

```r
library(lubridate)
raw <- raw |> mutate(
  enroll_date = parse_date_time(
    enroll_date,
    orders = c("ymd","dmy","d-b-Y")) |>
  as_date())
sum(is.na(raw$enroll_date))
```

```{.text .code-output}
[1] 0
```

::: {.code-note}
orders lists the formats to try, in priority order.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: lubridate's parse\_date\_time tries each format in turn, taming mixed entry styles.

Misconception: dates are just text - stored as text they cannot be sorted or differenced.

Clinical interpretation: a real Date lets you compute follow-up time and check enrolment windows.

Ask: why check sum(is.na(enroll\_date)) afterwards? Expected: a spike means a format we did not list and must add.

Demo tip: feed parse\_date\_time a few sample strings to show each order matching.
:::

## Factors and Reference Levels {.smaller}

### Factors give categories structure

| factor() stores categories with defined levels.
| Ordered factors keep ordinal meaning (education, activity).
| Levels control the order in tables and plots.

### Set the reference level deliberately

| For binary outcomes, list 'No' first.
| factor(treatment\_uptake, levels = c("No","Yes"))
| The first level is the comparison baseline in models.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why 'No' first
Odds ratios then read as the odds of Yes versus No - the natural clinical direction.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: the first factor level is the reference, and it sets how every odds ratio is interpreted.

Misconception: level order is cosmetic - it silently flips the direction of model estimates.

Clinical interpretation: with 'No' as reference, OR \> 1 means higher odds of the outcome, as clinicians expect.

Ask: what does an OR of 3.56 for diabetes mean with 'No' as reference? Expected: diabetics have 3.56 times the odds of treatment uptake versus non-diabetics.

Demo tip: refit with levels reversed to show the OR invert to 1/3.56.
:::

## Demo: Final Missing-Data Audit

```r
colSums(is.na(analysis_data)) |>
  sort(decreasing = TRUE) |>
  head(12)
```

```{.text .code-output}
adherence        411
bp_controlled    411
bmi               18
sbp_mmhg          12
age                9
```

::: {.code-note}
adherence and bp\_controlled are NA by design for untreated patients.
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: audit missingness per column and distinguish structural NA from data problems.

Misconception: all NA is bad - adherence is undefined for someone not on treatment, so its NA is expected.

Clinical interpretation: only patients on treatment can have an adherence or BP-control status.

Ask: should we impute adherence for untreated patients? Expected: no - it is structurally missing, not unknown.

Demo tip: cross-tabulate adherence missingness against treatment\_uptake to show the by-design pattern.
:::

## Saving the Clean Data: the Contract

### Save once, reuse all week

| saveRDS keeps factor types and levels intact.
| write\_csv gives a human-readable backup.
| Days 3, 4 and 5 all start from this one file.

### The commands

| saveRDS(analysis\_data, "Data/analysis\_data.rds")
| write\_csv(analysis\_data, "Data/analysis\_data.csv")

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reload later
analysis\_data \<- readRDS("Data/analysis\_data.rds")
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: the saved .rds is the single source of truth for the rest of the course.

Misconception: CSV preserves everything - it loses factor levels and ordering, so .rds is the analysis file.

Clinical interpretation: a fixed clean dataset makes every later result reproducible and auditable.

Ask: why prefer .rds over .csv for the analysis? Expected: it restores factors and ordered levels exactly, no re-cleaning needed.

Demo tip: save, clear the workspace, then readRDS to prove the factors survive.
:::

## Common Mistakes and Debugging

### Watch for these

| Forgetting na= so 999 enters as a real number.
| Wrong factor level order flipping every odds ratio.
| Letting NA fall through case\_when to the wrong group.

::: {.callout-important}
## NA propagation
Any arithmetic with NA returns NA; check is.na before computing.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Debug habit
After each step run summary() or table(..., useNA = "ifany").
:::

::: {.notes}
Key point: most cleaning bugs are silent; build the habit of inspecting after every step.

Misconception: no error message means the step worked - wrong results often run without complaint.

Clinical interpretation: a silently mis-coded outcome can change the entire study conclusion.

Ask: how would you catch a forgotten na= argument? Expected: an implausible max in summary(), e.g. an SBP of 999.

Demo tip: trigger each mistake live, then show the diagnostic that catches it.
:::

## Day 2 Exercise: Clean the Simulated Dataset {.smaller}

[Work in Practicals/day2\_exercise.R and mirror today's pipeline.]{.slide-intro}

- Import the raw CSV with the correct na= sentinels.
- Remove duplicate records with distinct(); confirm 1500 rows.
- Recode sex to Female/Male; standardise the Yes/No binaries.
- Apply plausible ranges; set impossible values to NA.
- Recompute BMI; derive bmi\_cat and bp\_category.
- Parse enroll\_date; set factors and reference levels.
- Run the final missing-data audit and explain each NA.
- Save the result to Data/analysis\_data.rds.

::: {.notes}
Key point: the exercise reproduces the full contract so each participant ends with an identical clean file.

Misconception: skipping a step is fine if numbers 'look ok' - later days will fail to load a wrong-typed file.

Clinical interpretation: the expected end state is the validated dataset used for all later analyses.

Ask: how will you know your file is correct? Expected: 1500 rows, clean factors, and the audit matching the demo counts.

Demo tip: have them readRDS their own file and glimpse() it to self-check against yours.
:::
